card.title: Digital menu vs paper menu: what each really costs a restaurant
card.excerpt: Printing is only the visible part. We compare the full cost of paper and digital menus — updates, translations, mistakes and lost orders — with real numbers.

h1: Digital menu vs paper menu: what each really costs a restaurant
intro: Every restaurant starts with a paper menu — and most keep paying for it long after it stops making sense. This comparison breaks down what paper actually costs once you count reprints, translations and slower service, and where a [QR digital menu](route:/digital-menu) wins or loses.

blocks.text: A mid-size menu (8–12 pages, laminated, 30 copies) costs **€150–€400** per print run. Most venues reprint 3–6 times a year: seasonal dishes, price changes, worn-out pages. That is €450–€2,400 a year just to keep paper current — and every price change you postpone because "we just printed" is margin you quietly lose.
A digital menu has no print run. You change a price and it is live in seconds, on every table at once.
The hidden costs: where paper really loses

items: **Stale prices.** With paper, a supplier price hike waits weeks for the next reprint. Digital updates the same day.
**Translations.** Tourist areas need 2–5 languages. On paper that multiplies pages and print costs; a digital menu translates every item automatically.
**86'd items.** Paper can't show that a dish ran out — guests order it, staff apologise. Digital hides sold-out items in one tap.
**Photos.** Menu photos sell, but photo-heavy paper menus are expensive to print well. Digital shows a photo for every dish for free.
**Hygiene and wear.** Laminated menus get sticky and scratched; guests notice.

blocks.text: Keep 2–3 paper copies for guests who prefer them. The point isn't zero paper — it's that paper stops being the thing you maintain.

Honesty helps here: a one-page tasting menu that changes monthly, a fine-dining room where phones feel out of place, or a regulars-only bar with six items — paper is fine there. The economics flip when your menu is long, changes often, needs languages or photos, or when guests order faster than your floor staff can walk.

items.q: Do guests need to install an app?
items.a: No. The QR code opens the menu in the phone's browser — nothing to install, no sign-up.

items.q: What happens if a guest doesn't have a smartphone?
items.a: Keep a few paper copies at the host stand. In practice fewer than 5% of guests ask for one.

items.q: Can a digital menu take orders too?
items.a: Yes — guests can order and pay from the table, and orders go straight to the [kitchen display](route:/kitchen-display). You can also run it as a view-only menu first.

items.q: How long does the setup take?
items.a: About 5 minutes: scan your paper menu, review the items, print the QR codes.
